claims.text: Homogeneous noble-metal HEA nanoparticle formation is governed by an interplay between precursor-reduction kinetics and limited atomic mobility.
Modestly slowing the thermal ramp improves alloy formation by allowing each metal to be incorporated before phase separation occurs.
The proposed starting material is a crystalline single-source precursor containing a homogeneous mixture of five noble-metal ions in coordination complexes.
The relevant reduction regime is an H2-containing atmosphere at approximately 500 °C.
Rapid heating limits the mobility of reduced metal atoms.
Limited free-atom mobility favors random single-phase alloy formation in systems containing many atom types.
Limited atomic mobility kinetically locks the elemental configuration before diffusion-driven phase segregation can occur.
Rapid reduction immobilizes atoms and ensures their prompt incorporation into nucleation sites.
Controlling the timing or steady-state availability of different metal precursors can alter the resulting HEA nanocrystal structure.
Changing the heat-up rate allows sequentially reduced metals to merge into a uniform alloy.
Excessively fast reduction can create local compositional fluctuations that cause phase separation.
Excessively slow processing permits atomic rearrangement into segregated phases.
A modulated, slower thermal ramp will produce a more homogeneous single-phase alloy than the rapid-heating baseline.
The modulated ramp will produce nanoparticles with greater surface-atom exposure than the rapid-heating baseline.
Rapid, unmodulated reduction is typically prone to local atomic imbalance, phase separation, or uncontrolled morphology.
The mechanism is intended to apply to low-temperature reduction of constrained solid precursors containing five or more noble metals.
The mechanism may not apply to solution syntheses with higher atomic mobility or to systems containing fewer elements.
Catalytic activity can be used as a proxy for nanoparticle surface-atom exposure.

contradictions.description: Rapid reduction is described both as immobilizing atoms and ensuring incorporation into nucleation sites and as causing local imbalances and phase separation. An implied optimum could reconcile these statements, but no operational distinction between beneficially rapid and excessively rapid reduction is defined.

The cited NiPdPt pyrolysis record reports the opposite ramp-direction trend: fast moving-bed pyrolysis formed an alloy without segregation, whereas slower processing produced phase separation. It therefore does not support the prediction that slowing the baseline ramp improves homogeneity.
